[Event "e4"]

1. e4 { The King's Pawn takes two central squares at once, d5 and f5, and opens the way for the queen and the light-squared bishop. It is the most played first move at every level: the game tends to open up quickly, with fast development and early tactics. Black's main answers all fight for the center in their own way: [e5] meets the pawn head-on, [c5] (the Sicilian) attacks d4 from the side, while [e6] and [c6] prepare [d5] to challenge e4 directly. [%csl Gd5,Gf5][%cal Ge2e4] } 1... c5 ( 1... e5 ) ( 1... e6 ) *

[Event "e4 e5"]

1. e4 e5 { The Open Game: Black copies White, claims an equal share of the center and frees the dark-squared bishop and the queen. The pawn on e5 stops White from simply playing [d4] for a big center without a trade. The usual way on is [Nf3], which develops while attacking e5 and leads to the classical openings (Italian, Ruy Lopez, Scotch). [Bc4] aims at f7 straight away, [Nc3] keeps things quiet, and [f4], the King's Gambit, gives a pawn to tear Black's center down. [%csl Gd4][%cal Ge7e5,Gg1f3] } 2. Nf3 ( 2. Bc4 ) ( 2. Nc3 ) *

[Event "e4 e5 Nf3"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 { The knight comes out to its best square, attacks the pawn on e5 and gets White one step closer to castling. Black has to look after that pawn. [Nc6] is the natural way, developing a piece at the same time. [Nf6], the Petrov, counterattacks e4 instead, and [d6], the Philidor, defends with a pawn: solid, but it shuts in the bishop on f8. Defending with [f6] is a known mistake: it takes the knight's best square and weakens the diagonal to the king, and [Nxe5] is already strong. [%cal Gf3e5,Gb8c6,Gg8f6] } 2... Nc6 ( 2... Nf6 ) ( 2... d6 ) *

[Event "e4 e5 Nf3 d6"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 { The Philidor Defence, recommended by Ruy López de Segura in 1561 to avoid the pin of [w:Bb5] after [b:Nc6] and made famous by François-André Danican Philidor in his 1749 treatise. Protecting e5 with [d6] builds a sturdy pawn chain and leaves Black's c-pawn free to advance, at the cost of boxing in the dark-squared bishop on f8. [d4] challenges the centre directly, [Bc4] targets f7 first, and [Nc3], [c3] or [d3] build more quietly. [%csl Ye5,Yf8,Yf7][%cal Gd2d4] } 3. d4 ( 3. Bc4 ) ( 3. Nc3 ) ( 3. c3 ) ( 3. d3 ) ( 3. Bb5+ ) ( 3. h3 ) *

[Event "e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 { White strikes at e5 immediately, threatening [dxe5] followed by trading queens on d8 to win a central pawn and strip Black's castling rights. Black has three main replies: [exd4] is the solid Exchange Variation, surrendering the centre to free Black's pieces; [Nd7] is Hanham's Variation, holding the e5 strongpoint; and [Nf6] is Nimzowitsch's counterattack against e4. [Bg4] is the dubious pin from Morphy's 1858 Opera Game. [%csl Ye5,Yd8,Ye4][%cal Ge5d4] } 3... exd4 ( 3... Nd7 ) ( 3... Nf6 ) ( 3... Bg4 ) ( 3... f5 ) *

[Event "e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Bg4 { The third move of the 1858 Paris Opera Game between Paul Morphy and the consulting Duke Karl of Brunswick and Count Isouard. Black pins f3 hoping to hold e5 without giving up the centre, yet the pin fails tactically: White captures [dxe5] at once, forcing Black either to give up the bishop pair on f3 or drop a clean central pawn. [%csl Yf3,Ye5][%cal Gd4e5] } 4. dxe5 *

[Event "e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Bg4 4. dxe5 { White opens the d-file, so Black cannot recapture [dxe5] without losing a pawn to [Qxd8+] and [Nxe5]. Black must either concede the bishop pair as in Morphy's Opera Game with [Bxf3] ([Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4]) or try the Albin-Blackburne Gambit [Nd7], sacrificing a pawn via [Nd7 exd6 Bxd6 Nc3 Ngf6 Be2] to catch up in kingside development. Whichever way Black plays on move four, White's open d-file and lead in development keep Black's king under pressure. [%cal Gg4f3] } 4... Bxf3 ( 4... Nd7 ) *

[Event "e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Bg4 4. dxe5 Bxf3 { As in Morphy's Opera Game, Black trades off the knight on f3 before recapturing on e5 so no pawn falls on the spot. White recaptures [Qxf3], bringing the queen to an active post that eyes both f7 and b3 without fear of harassment; Géza Maróczy's endgame squeeze [gxf3 dxe5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 f4] is a strong alternative that uses the two bishops in a queenless middlegame. [%csl Yf3,Ye5,Yf7][%cal Gd1f3] } 5. Qxf3 *

[Event "e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Bg4 4. dxe5 Bxf3 5. Qxf3 { White recaptures with the queen, keeping the kingside pawns whole while aiming down the f-file toward f7 and standing ready to slide to b3 once the light-squared bishop develops. Black recovers the central pawn with [dxe5], hoping to bring out [b:Nf6], [b:Bd6] or [b:Qf6] before White's unopposed light-squared bishop locks onto Black's weak light squares. Once Black recaptures on e5, [w:Bc4] seizes the a2-g8 diagonal with immediate mating and fork threats. [%csl Yf7][%cal Gd6e5,Gf3f7] } 5... dxe5 *

[Event "e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Bg4 4. dxe5 Bxf3 5. Qxf3 dxe5 { Material is level, yet White has an active queen, an open d-file and the unopposed bishop pair while every black piece still sits on the back rank. Morphy's continuation [Bc4] threatens checkmate in one on f7 and sets up the [Qb3] double attack on f7 and b7, forcing Black onto the defensive before a single minor piece can develop normally. [%csl Rf7,Yb7][%cal Gf1c4] } 6. Bc4 *

[Event "e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Bg4 4. dxe5 Bxf3 5. Qxf3 dxe5 6. Bc4 { White threatens [Qxf7#] on the spot. To avoid losing a pawn or getting tied in knots by [Qb3], Black must guard f7 while keeping the f8-bishop unblocked with [Qf6] ([Qf6 Qb3 Bc5 O-O Bb6]) or [Qd7] ([Qd7 Qb3 c6]), avoiding the Duke and Count's Opera-Game mistake [Nf6] which left b7 unguarded and forced the clumsy [b:Qe7]. Even against accurate queen defence, White castles short and brings [w:Nc3] and [w:Rd1] into play with a clear edge. [%csl Rf7,Yb7][%cal Gd8f6,Gd8d7] } 6... Qf6 ( 6... Qd7 ) *

[Event "e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Bg4 4. dxe5 Bxf3 5. Qxf3 dxe5 6. Bc4 Nf6 $2 { The exact slip of the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard against Morphy in 1858. Blocking with [Nf6] leaves b7 undefended to [Qb3], hitting f7 and b7 at once and forcing [Qe7] which boxes in Black's f8-bishop (allowing [Qxb7] or Morphy's [Nc3]). Defend with [Qf6] or [Qd7]. } 7. Qb3 *

[Event "e4"]

1. e4 { Le pion du roi prend deux cases centrales d'un coup, d5 et f5, et ouvre la voie à la dame et au fou de cases blanches. C'est le premier coup le plus joué à tous les niveaux : la partie s'ouvre vite, avec un développement rapide et de la tactique tôt. Les grandes réponses des Noirs luttent toutes pour le centre à leur façon : [e5] répond de front, [c5] (la Sicilienne) attaque d4 par le côté, tandis que [e6] et [c6] préparent [d5] pour contester e4 directement. [%csl Gd5,Gf5][%cal Ge2e4] } 1... c5 ( 1... e5 ) ( 1... e6 ) *

[Event "e4 e5"]

1. e4 e5 { La partie ouverte : les Noirs copient les Blancs, réclament leur part du centre et libèrent le fou de cases noires et la dame. Le pion e5 empêche les Blancs de jouer simplement [d4] pour un grand centre sans échange. La suite habituelle est [Nf3], qui développe en attaquant e5 et mène aux ouvertures classiques (Italienne, Espagnole, Écossaise). [Bc4] vise f7 tout de suite, [Nc3] garde un jeu calme, et [f4], le Gambit du Roi, donne un pion pour démolir le centre noir. [%csl Gd4][%cal Ge7e5,Gg1f3] } 2. Nf3 ( 2. Bc4 ) ( 2. Nc3 ) *

[Event "e4 e5 Nf3"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 { Le cavalier sort sur sa meilleure case, attaque le pion e5 et rapproche les Blancs du roque. Les Noirs doivent s'occuper de ce pion. [Nc6] est la façon naturelle, en développant une pièce au passage. [Nf6], la Petrov, contre-attaque plutôt e4, et [d6], la Philidor, défend avec un pion : solide, mais le fou de f8 reste enfermé. Défendre par [f6] est une erreur connue : le coup prend la meilleure case du cavalier et affaiblit la diagonale du roi, et [Nxe5] est déjà fort. [%cal Gf3e5,Gb8c6,Gg8f6] } 2... Nc6 ( 2... Nf6 ) ( 2... d6 ) *
